Terms act as a logical clock in Raft, letting servers detect obsolete information such as stale leaders; a server that sees a higher term updates its own, and a request with a stale term is rejected.

at.step: Reveal: terms as a logical clock

items.item: A voter grants its vote only if the candidate's log is at least as up-to-date as its own, compared by last term first and log length as a tiebreaker; this restriction is what guarantees Leader Completeness.

at.step: Reveal: the voting restriction

items.item: If two logs contain an entry with the same index and term, the logs are identical in all entries up through that index, maintained by AppendEntries's consistency check on every append.

at.step: Reveal: the log matching property, enforced on every append

items.item: Raft never commits log entries from previous terms by counting replicas; only an entry from the leader's current term is committed this way, and once it is, every prior entry is committed indirectly through the Log Matching property.

at.step: Reveal: why counting replicas of an old-term entry is unsafe

items.item: The paper's own worked scenario shows an entry from an earlier term sitting on a majority of servers while still being safe for a later candidate with a higher last term to overwrite.

at.step: Reveal: why counting replicas of an old-term entry is unsafe

items.item: Changing cluster membership routes through a transitional joint-consensus configuration requiring majorities of both the old and new configurations at once, to guarantee safety during the transition.

at.step: Reveal: joint consensus for membership change

items.item: Raft produces a result equivalent to Multi-Paxos and is as efficient, but its structure makes it simpler and more understandable; the two algorithms have identical decision-making power.

at.step: Recap

items.item: An entry sitting on only two of five servers when its leader crashes is not committed, because commitment requires a majority, and the new leader is free to overwrite it.

at.step: Predict: is that entry committed, and can the new leader overwrite it?

items.item: Once a leader's own current-term entry reaches a majority, that entry is committed instantly, independent of whether the leader survives to announce it, because any future candidate missing it fails the voting restriction's check against every server that holds it.

at.step: Prove it: the leader's own current-term entry just reached a majority, then it crashes — is the new leader free to overwrite it?
